target.title: feat: let agents remember across private conversations
target.body:
Closes #99611

## What Problem This Solves

Personal agents currently keep every private conversation isolated, so relevant context from another Telegram DM, WebUI session, TUI session, or other private surface is unavailable unless operators broaden session-tool visibility or assemble several advanced memory settings.

This leaves Owners without a safe, understandable choice between keeping conversations separate and allowing a trusted personal agent to remember relevant context across its private conversations.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds a default-off, per-agent `memorySearch.rememberAcrossConversations` setting. It reuses Memory Core for transcript indexing and authorization and Active Memory for bounded pre-reply retrieval, carrying a runtime-only trusted recall context rather than widening `tools.sessions.visibility` or merging transcripts.

The privacy boundary is fail-closed: recall is limited to the same agent's other recognized private conversations. The current conversation, groups, channels, global/shared sessions, other agents, internal/helper sessions, unknown identities, sandbox-denied sessions, and transcripts with shared aliases are excluded. Ordinary memory search/get callers retain their configured corpus; recall-only builtin and QMD transcript indexes are accessible only when trusted recall explicitly requests session sources.

## User Impact

Owners can opt a personal or fully trusted agent into **Remember across conversations** while preserving separate conversations and delivery routes. Existing agents keep **Keep conversations separate** behavior because the setting defaults to off.

Shared workspace Markdown memory is unchanged. Group and channel conversations remain isolated in both directions. `/active-memory off` pauses recall for one conversation, and indexing/search failures or timeouts do not block the user's reply.

## Evidence

- `pnpm test <15 affected test files> -- --reporter=dot` — **906/906 passed** across config, agent plumbing, Memory Core, Active Memory, QMD, doctor, Plugin SDK, and QA Lab suites.
- Builtin and QMD ordinary-search regressions were verified RED with the production source clamp temporarily removed, then GREEN after restoration.
- `pnpm openclaw qa suite --provider-mode mock-openai --scenario remember-across-conversations --output-dir .artifacts/qa-e2e/remember-pr-final` — **1/1 passed** against a real Gateway child and qa-channel transport. The scenario proves positive private-to-private recall plus group/anchor exclusion, setting-off behavior, per-conversation pause, fresh-conversation independence, and unchanged `tools.sessions.visibility`.
- `pnpm build` — passed.
- `pnpm config:docs:check` — passed.
- `pnpm plugin-sdk:api:check` — passed.
- Exact local child form of `pnpm check:changed` — passed all production/test typechecks, lint shards, import-cycle checks, architecture/security/package guards, and extension contracts.
- `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD` — passed.
- Final Codex autoreview — no findings; patch correct (0.88).

Live `openai/gpt-5.4 --fast` acceptance was not run locally because no approved API credential was available. The deterministic mock-provider scenario covers the complete Gateway/channel/privacy flow without provider variance.

target.title: fix(plugin-sdk): guard provider isConfigured probe against malformed config throws
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`resolveConfiguredCapabilityProvider` calls the `isProviderConfigured` callback without try/catch. When a realtime transcription provider (e.g. gradium) throws from its `isConfigured` implementation on an invalid baseUrl, the exception crashes capability resolution. Other usable providers are hidden behind one broken one.

This is the third sibling of #108569 which fixed the same throw-in-isConfigured pattern.

## Why This Change Was Made

Wrap the callback in try/catch. A thrown exception returns `{ ok: false, code: "provider-not-configured" }` — the same result as an unconfigured provider — so other providers remain selectable.

## User Impact

A single misconfigured realtime transcription provider no longer crashes voice-call media streaming initialization.

## Evidence

- `src/plugin-sdk/provider-selection-runtime.ts` — `resolveConfiguredCapabilityProvider`: try/catch around `isProviderConfigured` callback
- `pnpm test src/plugin-sdk/provider-selection-runtime.test.ts` — 4 passed, 0 regressions

target.title: fix(secrets): surface degradation in logs and doctor
target.body:
Related: #101265

## What Problem This Solves

SecretRef degradation can leave one owner cold at startup or keep a stale last-known-good value after reload, but the primary operator signal was easy to miss and could expose low-level resolution text.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Emits a warning-level structured `secrets.degraded` log at startup and reload with redacted owner kind, owner id, reason, cold/stale state, and the `openclaw secrets reload` retry hint.
- Keeps exact owner isolation: a failed webhook route stays cold while unrelated routes remain available.
- Makes doctor list degraded owners with the same redacted reason and retry guidance.
- Attributes typed reload failures to the actual failed owner; an unmapped typed failure reports conservative `unknown:unmapped` / cold metadata without leaking the SecretRef id.

Per maintainer decision, this PR adds no `secrets.degraded[]` gateway protocol/status field, schema, generated Swift model, protocol version bump, config option, parameter, environment variable, UI, or new capability.

## User Impact

Operators get a loud signal in the existing web UI log view and a human-readable doctor section. Public webhook requests remain generic `401 unauthorized`; secret values and SecretRef ids are not logged.

target.title: fix(baseten): reject malformed model metadata numbers
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Baseten live model discovery trusted JavaScript numeric string forms from `/models` metadata. A malformed string such as `0x100000` or `3.2e4` could be accepted through `Number(...)` and override curated context-window, max-token, or pricing metadata instead of falling back to the bundled catalog values.

## Why This Change Was Made

Live metadata now accepts JSON numbers as before, but string metadata must be canonical decimal syntax before it is parsed. Invalid numeric strings are ignored, so the existing fallback metadata remains authoritative for malformed live rows.

## User Impact

Baseten model catalogs no longer surface inflated or malformed live context windows, token limits, or per-token prices when the provider response contains non-decimal numeric strings.

## Evidence

- Current head: `175639afcba20f864b3b9232e6c6342522c415cf`.
- Provider-boundary transcript at the Baseten discovery seam passed for the current head: `discoverBasetenModels` used a redacted fetch guard for `https://inference.baseten.co/v1/models` with `Authorization: Bearer <redacted>`.
- The transcript fed a malformed `thinkingmachines/inkling` row with `context_length: "0x100000"`, `max_completion_tokens: "3.2e4"`, and malformed price strings `"0x1"`, `"4.2e-6"`, and `" 0.00000018 "`; the projected model kept bundled fallback values `contextWindow: 1048000`, `maxTokens: 32000`, and cost `{ input: 1, output: 4.05, cacheRead: 0.17, cacheWrite: 0 }`.
- The same transcript fed a supported canonical row with `context_length: "64000"`, `max_completion_tokens: 4000`, and decimal prices `"0.0000002"`, `0.0000008`, and `"0.00000004"`; the projected model applied live values `contextWindow: 64000`, `maxTokens: 4000`, and cost `{ input: 0.2, output: 0.8, cacheRead: 0.04, cacheWrite: 0 }`.
- Transcript assertions passed: `malformedFallsBack: true` and `supportedDecimalApplies: true`.

target.title: fix(tlon): bound auth response draining
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where successful Tlon / Urbit login responses could make `openclaw` drain an arbitrarily large or slowly streaming response body before returning the authentication cookie.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Tlon auth path still performs a best-effort body drain for Urbit setups that finalize cookies after response consumption, but now bounds that compatibility drain by both a 64 KiB byte cap and one short overall drain deadline. When either bound is reached, the body is cancelled without waiting for a non-settling cancellation callback.

## User Impact

Users can still authenticate against normal Urbit responses, while oversized, stalled, or slow-trickling successful login bodies no longer keep the login flow tied to unbounded response consumption.

target.title: fix(qa-lab): bound credential payload reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

QA Lab credential add commands enforced `OPENCLAW_QA_CREDENTIAL_PAYLOAD_MAX_BYTES` with a file stat before reading the payload. A payload file could grow after that stat and before the read, which let the command read and parse data beyond the configured cap.

## Why This Change Was Made

The credential payload reader now opens the file, verifies the opened handle is a regular file, and reads at most `maxBytes + 1` bytes from that handle. That keeps boundary-sized payload JSON accepted while rejecting files that are oversized at stat time or grow past the cap before the read, without reading the whole grown file into memory.

## User Impact

Operators using QA Lab credential pools get the configured payload byte limit applied to the actual bytes consumed by the CLI. Oversized or racing payload files fail before any credential broker request is sent.

## Evidence

- Current head: `7ff257fb1484a66925de3a2ef1f8c44a59a2389e`.
- Docker Linux proof: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/qa-lab/src/cli.runtime.test.ts -- -t "credential payload"` passed in `node:24-bullseye`; the targeted file reported 4 passing tests and 101 skipped.
- `git diff --check -- extensions/qa-lab/src/cli.runtime.ts extensions/qa-lab/src/cli.runtime.test.ts` passed.

## Related independent bug-family PRs

This is an independent bounded-file-read fix for QA Lab credential payloads. It is not stacked on any sibling PR and has no merge dependency.

target.title: fix(pairing): normalize account key in legacy allowFrom filename parsing
target.body:
Closes #110187

## What Problem This Solves

The startup-migration gate refuses to report the gateway ready when a legacy allowFrom JSON file has a non-canonical account id segment in its filename (e.g. `telegram-HY_RIN_Bot-allowFrom.json` instead of `telegram-hy_rin_bot-allowFrom.json`). The `parseAllowFromFilename` parser cannot match it to any configured account, leaving the file unresolved. The file is never deleted, so every restart produces the same migration warning — a permanent crash loop with no in-product recovery path.

## Why This Change Was Made

`parseAllowFromFilename` compared the raw filename segment (`accountKey`) against `safeAccountKey(accountId)` without normalizing the segment first. The write path has always used `safeAccountKey` (lowercase + special-char replacement) to generate filenames, but the migration reader was not updated to apply the same normalization when parsing them. Codex review (July 17–18) on the linked issue confirmed: the parser mismatch is still present on current main, and `#108453` (default-account fallback) did not cover mixed-case or non-canonical account id spellings.

## User Impact

- Users upgrading with a legacy allowFrom file whose account segment is not in canonical `safeAccountKey` form no longer crash-loop
- The file is successfully migrated to SQLite and removed; no manual intervention needed
- Previously-working canonical filenames (e.g. `telegram-hy_rin_bot-allowFrom.json`) continue to resolve identically — `safeAccountKey` is idempotent on already-normalized inputs
- Ambiguous cases (two configured account ids that collide under `safeAccountKey`) remain unresolved with the same warning — no behavior change
- Non-canonical DEFAULT filenames (e.g. `telegram-DEFAULT-allowFrom.json`) that do not match any configured account remain unresolved; if a configured `"default"` account exists, `safeAccountKey("DEFAULT")` = `"default"` matches it and the file migrates normally

## Evidence

**Real environment**: Linux x86_64, Node v24.18.0, branch `fix/allowfrom-accountkey-normalize-110187`, current working tree

### End-to-end `autoMigrateLegacyState` proof

This exercises the same migration entry point used by `openclaw doctor --fix` and gateway startup (`src/commands/doctor-config-preflight.ts:586`).

**Scenario A: mixed-case HY_RIN_Bot + configured `hy_rin_bot` account → migrated, gateway can report READY**

```console
=== Scenario A: telegram-HY_RIN_Bot-allowFrom.json with configured hy_rin_bot ===

[state-migrations] Auto-migrated legacy state:
- Migrated 1 telegram/hy_rin_bot allowFrom entry → shared SQLite state
Changes: [
  "Migrated 1 telegram/hy_rin_bot allowFrom entry → shared SQLite state"
]
Warnings: []
File still exists: false
SQLite allowFrom: {
  "hy_rin_bot": [
    "1008"
  ]
}
RESULT A: PASS
```

**Scenario B: uppercase DEFAULT, no configured "default" account → file left in place, unresolved warning blocks readiness**

```console
=== Scenario B: telegram-DEFAULT-allowFrom.json without configured default ===

[state-migrations] Legacy state migration warnings:
- Legacy channel allowFrom channel/account is unresolved; left in place at /tmp/e2e-proof-b-xxx/.openclaw/credentials/telegram-DEFAULT-allowFrom.json
Changes: []
Warnings: [
  "Legacy channel allowFrom channel/account is unresolved; left in place at ..."
]
File still exists: true
RESULT B: PASS (unresolved, as expected)
```

**Scenario C: uppercase DEFAULT + configured "default" account → migrated successfully**

```console
=== Scenario C: telegram-DEFAULT-allowFrom.json WITH configured default account ===

[state-migrations] Auto-migrated legacy state:
- Migrated 1 telegram/default allowFrom entry → shared SQLite state
Changes: [
  "Migrated 1 telegram/default allowFrom entry → shared SQLite state"
]
Warnings: []
File still exists: false
SQLite allowFrom: {
  "default": [
    "1010"
  ]
}
RESULT C: PASS
```

### Scenario Matrix

Filename segment | Configured accounts | `safeAccountKey(segment)` | Expected | Result
---|---|---|---|---
`hy_rin_bot` (canonical) | `["hy_rin_bot"]` | `hy_rin_bot` | MATCH → `hy_rin_bot` | ✅
`HY_RIN_Bot` (mixed-case, #110187) | `["hy_rin_bot"]` | `hy_rin_bot` | MATCH → `hy_rin_bot` | ✅
`My_Work_Bot` (underscore-bearing mixed-case) | `["my_work_bot"]` | `my_work_bot` | MATCH → `my_work_bot` | ✅
`default` (no config) | `[]` | `default` | MATCH via fallback (literal `accountKey === "default"`) | ✅
`DEFAULT` (uppercase, no config) | `[]` | `default` | UNRESOLVED (no configured match, non-literal default) | ✅
`DEFAULT` (uppercase, with `"default"` account) | `["default"]` | `default` | MATCH → `default` (via configured-account filter) | ✅
`ops_bot` (ambiguous collision) | `["ops/bot", "ops_bot"]` | `ops_bot` | AMBIGUOUS (file kept) | ✅
`unknown` (unrelated) | `["hy_rin_bot"]` | `unknown` | UNRESOLVED (file kept) | ✅
`(empty)` (pathological) | `["hy_rin_bot"]` | (throw) | SKIP (safe, no throw) | ✅

### Test output (10 channel-pairing migration tests, all pass)

```console
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/state-migrations.channel-pairing.test.ts --run

 ✓ |infra| src/infra/state-migrations.channel-pairing.test.ts (10 tests) 1921ms
     ✓ imports pairing requests and scoped allowFrom entries into SQLite
     ✓ imports a built-in channel's explicit default account without channel config
     ✓ merges with authoritative SQLite rows and keeps unreadable sources
     ✓ leaves ambiguous sanitized account filenames in place
     ✓ does not infer default accounts for external channels
     ✓ imports allowFrom files with mixed-case account id segments
     ✓ imports underscore-bearing allowFrom files with mixed-case account id segments
     ✓ imports uppercase DEFAULT allowFrom files when a configured account matches
     ✓ leaves uppercase DEFAULT allowFrom files unresolved for bundled channels
     ✓ leaves overlapping channel and account filename interpretations in place

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  10 passed (10)
```

### Codex Review Resolution (July 18)

Finding | Status | Change
---|---|---
Legacy filename contract unverified on current main | ✅ Confirmed | Code archaeology across 6 commits: all write paths use `safeAccountKey`; read path was missing it
Accept the historical raw account-id spelling alongside the canonical safe key | ✅ Fixed | `safeAccountKey(accountKey)` normalizes both raw and canonical spellings before comparing
Ambiguity left unresolved and explicitly reported, not guessed | ✅ Preserved | `matchingAccountIds.length > 1` → ambiguous logic unchanged
Overly broad normalization could associate a legacy allowlist file with the wrong account | ✅ Safe | `safeAccountKey` deterministic; collision → ambiguous (file kept); `removeImportedSource` only on successful match
Whether raw legacy filenames are an intentional supported input | ✅ Addressed | Not intentional, but migration code reads user disk files; not tolerating causes permanent crash loop
Whether a matching state migration already landed | ✅ Verified | Only `5e41074009` (#108453) — different root cause
Add focused regression coverage for mixed-case and underscore-bearing Telegram account IDs | ✅ Added | 3 new tests
**[P1] Keep implicit default fallback canonical** — `normalizedAccountKey === DEFAULT_ACCOUNT_ID` broadened attribution | ✅ Fixed | Changed to `accountKey === DEFAULT_ACCOUNT_ID` (literal comparison); removed `isNonCanonicalDefault` guard that was overly broad — now the logic first matches configured accounts via `safeAccountKey` normalization, then falls back to the implicit bundled default only when the filename suffix is the literal `"default"` and no configured account matched

### Gateway startup crash-loop path (code trace)

1. `parseAllowFromFilename` returns `{ target: null, reason: "unresolved" }` — `src/infra/state-migrations.channel-pairing.ts:139`
2. `migrateLegacyChannelPairingState` pushes warning — `src/infra/state-migrations.channel-pairing.ts:271-274`
3. `channelPairing.warnings` merged into `autoMigrateLegacyState` result — `src/infra/state-migrations.doctor.ts:1265`
4. `noteStartupStateMigrationResult` pushes into `startupMigrationWarnings` — `src/commands/doctor-config-preflight.ts:413`
5. `startupMigrationWarnings.length > 0` → `throwStartupMigrationRefusal` — `src/commands/doctor-config-preflight.ts:624-630`
6. File is not deleted (unresolved → `continue`), so `hasLegacy: files.length > 0` is true on next restart — `src/infra/state-migrations.channel-pairing.ts:71`

**`src/infra/state-migrations.channel-pairing.ts`** (+15/-8):

- Normalize `accountKey` via `safeAccountKey` before comparing with configured account ids
- Wrap in try/catch so pathological filename segments skip safely instead of throwing
- Match configured accounts first (including `"default"` accounts that `safeAccountKey` maps from e.g. `"DEFAULT"`); then fall back to the implicit bundled-default only when `accountKey === DEFAULT_ACCOUNT_ID` (literal) and no configured account matched
- Removed `isNonCanonicalDefault` guard that blocked configured `"default"` accounts from matching non-canonical DEFAULT filenames

**`src/infra/state-migrations.channel-pairing.test.ts`** (+83):

- Added `imports allowFrom files with mixed-case account id segments` — `telegram-HY_RIN_Bot-allowFrom.json` + configured `hy_rin_bot`
- Added `imports underscore-bearing allowFrom files with mixed-case account id segments` — `telegram-My_Work_Bot-allowFrom.json` + configured `my_work_bot`

- Default-account fallback for bundled channels (`CHANNEL_IDS` + literal `DEFAULT_ACCOUNT_ID` check)

The logic now correctly handles configured `"default"` accounts matching non-canonical DEFAULT filenames (e.g. Telegram's auto-provided `"default"` account), while the implicit bundled-default fallback is restricted to the literal `"default"` suffix only when no configured account matched. target.title: improve(ui): live pref sync, composer model provenance, Agent Defaults rename, Memory Import restyle
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Four follow-ups from the settings restructure (#110445):

1. Agent-approved pref changes (theme, language, …) only applied after a reconnect or a settings-page visit — other connected clients had no way to learn config changed.
2. The chat composer's model picker looked identical whether a session was using the Settings default or overriding it, and offered no way back to the default (reasoning already had both).
3. The "AI & Agents" settings page read as a sibling of the per-agent "Agents" manager while actually holding schema-backed global defaults.
4. Memory Import was the last settings-adjacent page on fully bespoke card markup instead of the settings design language.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Live pref sync:** the gateway now broadcasts a hash-only `config.changed` event (operator.read scoped, registered in the event scope guards) after every persisted config write (`config.set`/`patch`/`apply`). The Control UI refreshes its config snapshot on the event — skipped while a local settings draft has unsaved edits — so `ui.prefs` changes made by an agent or another device apply live everywhere. Config content never rides the event; readers fetch via `config.get`.
- **Model provenance:** the combined model/reasoning picker gains a provenance row mirroring the reasoning anatomy — muted "Using default from Settings" when inherited, "Session override" with an icon reset (commits the empty override) when not.
- **Agent Defaults:** rename only (route/path unchanged); title and subtitle now say what the page is: global agent defaults (models, skills, tools, memory, session).
- **Memory Import:** intro, provider sections, path rows, replace toggle, status badges, and empty states now render through `settings-ui` primitives; only the collection review list, apply report, skeleton, and confirm dialog keep custom markup. Dead bespoke CSS pruned (net −21 LOC).

## User Impact

- Change the theme from your phone or ask the agent to — every open Control UI follows within a second, no reload.
- The composer tells you when a session is off the default model and gets you back in one click.
- Settings nav reads unambiguously; Memory Import looks like every other settings surface.

## Evidence

- New scope-guard test for `config.changed` in `src/gateway/gateway-misc.test.ts`; all 99 gateway server-method test files green (2003 tests). Chat picker suites green (385 tests incl. provenance selectors). Memory Import tests green (12; load-bearing selectors kept). i18n baseline/verify clean.
- Codex autoreview (`gpt-5.6-sol`, xhigh): clean first pass — "no accepted/actionable findings", verdict "patch is correct".
- Remote `check:changed` gates run on this head (typecheck core/tests/UI, lint, format, plugin-SDK manifest, i18n catalog).

## Summary

Fixes #109985

Two fixes:
1. **qa-lab: cancel unread response body on HTTP error** — call `response.body?.cancel()` before throwing on non-2xx responses in `getJson`/`getJsonNoStore` so the connection is released back to the pool.
2. **vertex-adc: guard JSON.parse against malformed credential files** — wrap `JSON.parse` in try-catch with a descriptive error message instead of a raw SyntaxError.

## Real behavior proof

### 1. qa-lab response body cancel

**Behavior addressed**: When an HTTP error response (4xx/5xx) was received, `response.json()` was never called but the response body was left unconsumed, holding the connection open.

**Real environment tested**: Node.js test runner (vitest) with mocked `fetch`.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:


**After-fix evidence**:
```
Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  7 passed (7)
```

**Observed result after the fix**: Each non-2xx path calls `response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)`, covering:
- All error status codes (400, 403, 429, 500, 503) for both `getJson` and `getJsonNoStore`
- Null body (safe: optional chaining `?.`)
- Cancel rejection (suppressed by `.catch(() => undefined)`)

**What was not tested**: `postJson` was not modified — it calls `response.json()` on error to extract an error payload, so body cancel would interfere.

### 2. vertex-adc JSON.parse guard

target.title: feat(memory): add excludePaths option to memorySearch config
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Automated Dreaming/light/ content (low-confidence, high-volume) dominates memory search indexes. In our observed instance, `memory/dreaming/light/` accounts for **79% (179.9KB)** of indexed memory files - approximately 35KB/day of auto-generated content with uniform 0.58 confidence scores. This severely degrades memory search signal-to-noise ratio.

Users need a way to keep these files on disk (they're still useful for Dreaming) but exclude them from search indexing.

## Solution

New `memorySearch.excludePaths` field accepts workspace-relative glob patterns:

```json5
{
  agents: {
    defaults: {
      memorySearch: {
        excludePaths: ["memory/dreaming/light", "memory/archive/**"],
      },
    },
  },
}
```

Patterns are matched with **minimatch** (existing project dependency) against workspace-relative paths inside `memory/` and `extraPaths`.

**Scope note:** `excludePaths` currently only affects the **builtin** memory search indexing backend. QMD collections are not yet wired; this is clearly documented so QMD users are not promised behavior they will not get.

## Design Decisions

- **Filtering order**: `excludePaths` runs *after* `shouldSkipRootMemoryAuxiliaryPath` - built-in auxiliary-path filtering (e.g. `.openclaw-repair`) has higher priority
- **Path matching**: workspace-relative (e.g. `memory/dreaming/light`), not absolute
- **Glob support**: full minimatch wildcards (`**`, `*`, etc.)
- **Plain directory prefix**: passing a directory path like `memory/dreaming/light` (no glob chars) automatically matches all files under that directory
- **Backward compatible**: not passing `excludePaths` leaves behavior unchanged
- **CLI diagnostics**: `memory status` intentionally does NOT apply excludePaths - diagnostics should see all files

## Changes

- `src/config/types.tools.ts` - type definition
- `src/config/zod-schema.agent-runtime.ts` - zod validation
- `src/config/schema.help.ts` - help text
- `src/config/schema.labels.ts` - UI label
- `src/agents/memory-search.ts` - resolve in mergeConfig
- `packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/internal.ts` - core filtering logic with prefix + glob matching
- `extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-sync-ops.ts` - pass through from config
- `packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/internal.test.ts` - unit tests
- `docs/reference/memory-config.md` - documentation
- `src/config/schema.help.quality.test.ts` - help key verification

## Evidence

Unit tests cover:
- Exact directory path excludes files (`memory/dreaming/light`)
- Glob wildcard excludes directories (`memory/archive/**`)
- Empty/missing `excludePaths` returns all files (backward compat)
- Excluded paths are tested alongside non-excluded paths to confirm specificity

### Real Behavior Proof

```
npm test -- packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/internal.test.ts
```

**Result: 12/12 tests passed** ?

Manual `filterMinimatch` validation: **6/6 scenarios passed** ?

| Scenario | Expected | Result |
|----------|----------|--------|
| Exact dir match (`memory/dreaming/light`) | Excluded | ? |
| Glob wildcard (`memory/archive/**`) | Excluded | ? |
| Non-matching path retained | Included | ? |
| Empty excludePaths | All retained | ? |
| Mixed excluded + retained | Correct split | ? |
| Plain prefix w/o glob chars | Treated as dir prefix | ? |

Backward compat: empty `excludePaths` retains all files ?

Environment: Node.js v24.16.0, minimatch 10.2.5, Windows. CI check runs confirm no regressions.

target.title: fix(config): use Object.hasOwn in projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape to avoid prototype pollution
target.body:
## Summary
Replace `!(key in runtime)` with `!Object.hasOwn(runtime, key)` in `projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape` to prevent prototype pollution when config keys collide with inherited Object.prototype properties.

## What Problem This Solves
The `projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape` function in `src/config/io.write-prepare.ts:75` iterates over source config entries and checks whether each key is absent from the runtime config. The check uses the `in` operator, which traverses the prototype chain. If a config key collides with an `Object.prototype` property name (e.g. `"toString"`, `"constructor"`), `!(key in runtime)` incorrectly returns `false`, causing the code to enter the recursive `else` branch and call `projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape(sourceValue, runtime[key])` where `runtime[key]` resolves to a prototype function.

**Code evidence**: In `src/config/io.write-prepare.ts:75`, `!(key in runtime)` uses the `in` operator on a plain config object where `key` comes from `Object.entries(source)` — user-controlled data.

## Root Cause
- The `in` operator traverses the prototype chain; `Object.hasOwn` checks only own properties
- Config keys come from `Object.entries(source)` — user-controlled data
- The same function uses `Object.keys()` (own properties only) for iterating, creating an inconsistency
- The same file already has `Object.hasOwn(value, "$include")` at line 85 — this site was missed (path drift)

## Why This Fix
- **Chosen approach**: Replace `!(key in runtime)` with `!Object.hasOwn(runtime, key)` — a 1-line change
- **Consistent**: The same file uses `Object.hasOwn` at line 85 for `"$include"` and at lines 41-42 in `createMergePatch`
- **Zero overhead**: Identical performance characteristics
- **Reference PR**: Pattern matches #98503

## User Impact
- **Before**: A config key named `toString` or `constructor` would bypass the "new key" check and enter recursive projection with a prototype function
- **After**: Prototype-named keys are correctly treated as absent from runtime and kept as-is

## Evidence
- **Before**: `!("toString" in {})` returns `false` (prototype pollution causes wrong branch)
- **After**: `!Object.hasOwn({}, "toString")` returns `true` (correct — treated as new key)
- Regression test added: `projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape: treats prototype-named keys as absent in runtime`

## Real Behavior Proof

### Before (on main)
```bash
$ node --import tsx -e "
const { projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape } = await import('./src/config/io.write-prepare.ts');
const source = { toString: 'my-value' };
const runtime = {};
const result = projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape(source, runtime);
// With '!(key in runtime)': 'toString' in {} → true (prototype)
// Goes to else branch with runtime['toString'] = Object.prototype.toString
console.log('FAIL: typeof result.toString:', typeof result.toString);
"
# typeof result.toString: function (should be string)
```

### After (with fix)
```bash
$ node --import tsx -e "
const { projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape } = await import('./src/config/io.write-prepare.ts');
const source = { toString: 'my-value' };
const runtime = {};
const result = projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape(source, runtime);
console.log('PASS: result.toString:', result.toString);
"
# result.toString: my-value
```

## Tests and Validation
- `pnpm check` passed
- `npx vitest run src/config/io.write-prepare.test.ts` — 54 tests passed (53 existing + 1 regression)
- `git diff --check` clean
- New regression test: `projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape: treats prototype-named keys as absent in runtime`

target.title: fix(plugins): recurring plugin-scheduled jobs silently deleted after first post-boot agent turn
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Plugins that create recurring session turns through `api.session.workflow.scheduleSessionTurn` could lose those persistent cron jobs after normal post-boot plugin-registry churn. The row disappeared silently and the schedule did not fire again until a later restart re-seeded it.

## Root Cause

The original report correctly identified registry churn as the trigger, but the revised caller guard duplicated the compatibility lookup already performed by `ensureStandaloneRuntimePluginRegistryLoaded`, so both checks hit or missed together.

Gateway registries are also pinned for channel, HTTP, and session-extension surfaces. An agent-scoped active-registry replacement therefore does not directly retire the cron-owning Gateway registry.

The deletion path was cross-owner cleanup:

- Dynamic scheduled turns are indexed process-wide and carry their `ownerRegistry`.
- A different registry retiring for the same plugin ID could sweep those records without checking ownership.
- The cleanup callback then called `cron.remove()` on a job owned by the still-live pinned Gateway registry.
- Runtime scheduling, unscheduling, and attachment APIs also required exact active-registry identity even though their API lifecycle declares them late-callable. A pinned live registry therefore became unusable as soon as another registry became active.

## Fix

- Scope dynamic scheduler cleanup to the registry that is actually retiring.
- Preserve broad cleanup for non-registry lifecycle call sites.
- Let runtime workflow APIs operate while their registry is activated, loaded, guarded, and unretired, including when it remains live through a pinned surface.
- Continue rejecting calls before activation and after retirement.
- Leave loader compatibility, workspace, configuration, plugin-scope, and runtime-mode isolation unchanged.

## Evidence

Maintainer rewrite at `a83a53d4a16a6d0144948f3628bab144307886f5`:

- Owner-boundary regression proves retiring registry cleanup removes its own dynamic job while preserving the same-plugin job owned by another live registry, then removes that preserved job when its true owner retires.
- Pinned-registry contract proves schedule and unschedule remain live through active-registry churn, then fail closed after all pins release and the owner retires.
- Equivalent attachment lifecycle contract covers the other late-callable API using the same guard.
- `pnpm test src/plugins/contracts/scheduled-turns.contract.test.ts src/plugins/contracts/session-attachments.contract.test.ts src/plugins/runtime.test.ts`: 58 passed on Blacksmith Testbox.
- `pnpm check:changed`: passed core, core-test, extension, and extension-test typechecks; formatting; lint; plugin boundaries; import-cycle checks; and all selected guards.
- Fresh branch autoreview: clean, patch correct 0.89.
- The final hosted PR diff is five files, +143/-13. The superseded caller-guard source and mock-only tests are absent from the effective diff.

The focused suite initially caught an over-broad activation-in-progress guard; the final implementation now distinguishes an activated live registry from one still loading.

## Docs and Release Notes

No docs change is required; existing plugin SDK contracts already describe recurring scheduling and late-callable runtime APIs. `CHANGELOG.md` is release-owned.

Thanks to @danseerintel for the production report, diagnosis, and original reproduction work. Contributor credit is preserved in the maintainer rewrite.

---

AI-assisted PR. The final maintainer rewrite was source-reviewed against registry owners, cleanup callers, Gateway pins, scheduled-turn contracts, adjacent attachment contracts, and current `main`, then verified on Blacksmith Testbox.

target.title: fix(ai): keep OpenAI tool call id truncation UTF-16 safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`normalizeToolCallId` in `openai-completions.ts:1052` truncates oversized OpenAI tool call IDs with `id.slice(0, 40)`. When a tool call ID contains a UTF-16 surrogate pair straddling positions 39-40, `slice` splits the pair and leaves an unpaired high surrogate at position 39 — producing invalid Unicode in the outbound API request.

## Why This Change Was Made

`String.prototype.slice(0, 40)` operates on UTF-16 code units, not Unicode characters. A surrogate pair (e.g. 🐱 `\uD83D\uDC31`) consumes 2 code units. When the cut falls between the high and low surrogates, the result is invalid Unicode that downstream consumers (OpenAI API, JSON encoders, database storage) may reject.

The fix switches from `id.slice(0, 40)` to `truncateUtf16Safe(id, 40)` from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice`, an existing repo helper already used across the codebase for safe UTF-16 boundary truncation.

## Evidence Map

| Layer | Detail |
|-------|--------|
| **Changed surface** | `normalizeToolCallId` in `packages/ai/src/providers/openai-completions.ts:1052` — one line |
| **Fix** | `id.slice(0, 40)` → `truncateUtf16Safe(id, 40)` |
| **Sibling UTF-16 fix PRs** | #104054, #107664, #109561, #109498, #109839 — same helper, different surfaces |
| **Callers** | `convertMessages` → `streamOpenAICompletions` — cross-model tool-call path |
| **Test** | `openai-completions.test.ts` — 47/47 pass; new test with 41-code-unit 🐱 surrogate pair at boundary |
| **Mutation proof** | Reverting to `slice` makes the surrogate test fail with `trailing high surrogate: true` |
| **Before/after proof** | Terminal output below — `slice` produces `�` (invalid); `truncateUtf16Safe` drops both surrogates |

### Behavioral proof (terminal output)

```text
=== UTF-16 safe tool call id truncation proof ===

Input:    "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa🐱"
          length=41 code units

BEFORE (slice(0,40)):
  "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa�"
  length=40
  trailing high surrogate: true  ← BROKEN

AFTER (truncateUtf16Safe):
  "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"
  length=39
  trailing high surrogate: false
  prefix preserved: true

PASS: no unpaired surrogate in output
```

### Why a live API roundtrip is not practical

The `onPayload` hook in the test intercepts the exact JSON payload before `fetch` — the same bytes the API would receive. A live API call requires an active OpenAI key and is non-deterministic (rate limits, network). The test validates the `tool_call_id` field in that captured payload directly, which is stronger evidence than a live roundtrip.

### CI status

Rebased onto current `main` (`13ae897cfbd`). 47/47 tests pass locally. Surrogate-pair boundary test added; mutation check confirms the test catches the regression.

## User Impact

- Multi-model `openai` provider conversations with tool calls now produce valid Unicode in all tool call IDs
- No behavioral change for IDs without surrogate pairs at the boundary
- Non-OpenAI provider paths unchanged

target.title: refactor(state): move device identity into canonical SQLite state
target.body:
Related: #107227

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw still treated `identity/device.json` as the authoritative device identity store while global runtime state had moved to SQLite. That left a second mutable state owner, made Node and Apple clients persist the same Ed25519 identity differently, and kept runtime behavior coupled to a legacy sidecar.

## Why This Change Was Made

This moves the stable device identity keypair into the existing typed `device_identities` table in the shared state database. Runtime code reads and writes SQLite only. `openclaw doctor --fix` owns the one-time, validated JSON import: it claims the unchanged source, verifies the canonical row, then removes the legacy file. Node and Swift share canonical PEM key material and the same device ID derivation.

The change is additive at the database layer: it reuses the already-shipped table and does not advance `user_version`. It does not change the device ID, signing payload, Gateway wire format, CLI JSON shape, pairing model, or legacy import document. Device auth tokens remain a separate migration because their gateway-scoped key requires a different additive table.

## User Impact

Existing valid identities keep the same device ID and keys, so upgrades do not require re-pairing. Legacy files fail closed until Doctor performs the explicit migration. Invalid or conflicting material is preserved for diagnosis; Doctor can repair an invalid canonical row, with a new identity and reapproval only when the original key material cannot be recovered.

This is a one-way database-first cutover. After Doctor retires the JSON source, downgrading to an older JSON-only binary can create a different identity. Aligned upgrades are therefore required across processes sharing the state directory.

## Evidence

- Full changed-surface gate passed on Node 24.18.0: TypeScript checks, lint, focused test shards, database-first guards, import-cycle checks, and SwiftLint. The remote Testbox sync timed out before running code, so the trusted-source fallback ran locally under the repository-supported Node and Xcode toolchains.
- Focused Node proof: 43 tests passed across device identity, Doctor migration, and node identity CLI suites.
- Focused Swift proof: 25 `DeviceIdentityStoreTests` passed, including Node PEM interoperability, timestamp reconciliation, auth ownership conflicts, profile isolation, strict legacy validation, schema gates, and WAL behavior.
- SwiftLint: 0 violations across macOS, helpers, shared, and iOS sources.
- Source-blind CLI behavior validation exercised valid legacy refusal, explicit Doctor import, exact identity preservation in a later process, and malformed-source preservation.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- Fresh automated review found and drove fixes for corrupt-row recovery, migration races, Doctor mutation authority, metadata-only key rotation, native auth ownership conflicts, and Swift timestamp equality. The final whole-branch autoreview scanner then stopped before model invocation on synthetic device-key/test-token material; two independent read-only final reviews covered migration/race/security and Swift–Node interoperability instead.

target.title: fix(agents): short-circuit model fallback chain when result has delivery evidence (#108262)
target.body:
Closes #108262

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where the fallback chain short-circuits when a classified provider error (rate limit, overload, auth failure) surfaces as `finalAssistantVisibleText`. The `isSuccessfulResult` safety net treats any non-empty visible text as successful output, so the model never falls back — even though the text is a rendered error message, not genuine assistant output.

## Why This Change Was Made

Both the classifier at `result-fallback-classifier.ts:219-225` and `isSuccessfulResult` at `run-embedded-attempt.ts:292-296` assumed any non-empty visible text means successful output without checking whether the text came from error payloads. A provider error can surface as `finalAssistantVisibleText` from hook/reply machinery, but every text-bearing payload is an error block.

Two-part fix:
- Classifier: when `finalAssistantVisibleText` is non-empty, check payloads. If every text-bearing payload is an error or reasoning block, let the error payload check decide fallback instead of early-returning with `null`.
- `isSuccessfulResult`: when all payloads are error blocks, don't short-circuit fallback even if visible text is present.

Both guards require at least one non-error, non-reasoning payload with text before treating visible text as genuine assistant output.

## User Impact

When a provider returns a classified error (rate limit, auth denial, overload) that renders as visible text, OpenClaw correctly falls back to the next configured model. Previously the fallback chain was silently skipped, leaving the user with the provider error message.

## Evidence

### Production-function proof — three scenarios (redacted)

Directly exercises the production `classifyEmbeddedAgentRunResultForModelFallback` and the exact `isSuccessfulResult` implementation from `run-embedded-attempt.ts`.

```
═══ Scenario 1: Primary auth failure → fallback succeeds ═══

  → Primary model: zai/glm-5.1
  → finalAssistantVisibleText: REDACTED: {"success":false,"code":"CE-011",...}
  → Payload: isError=true
  ✅ PASS: Classifier returned non-null classification: {reason:"auth", code:"embedded_error_payload"}
  ✅ PASS: Classification reason is "auth"
  ✅ PASS: isSuccessfulResult returns false — fallback proceeds
  → Fallback model: openai/gpt-5.5
  ✅ PASS: isSuccessfulResult returns true for fallback result
  Fallback chain summary:
    Attempt 1: zai/glm-5.1  → auth error → classified reason=auth
    Attempt 2: openai/gpt-5.5 → success → delivered

═══ Scenario 2: Primary rate_limit → fallback succeeds ═══

  → Primary model: anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5
  → finalAssistantVisibleText: REDACTED: {"success":false,"code":"ER-429",...}
```

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where repeated Slack command menus could steadily increase Gateway memory during a long-running process. Every external-select menu retained its complete choice list for ten minutes, and the store had no limit on how many unexpired menus it could hold at once.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Slack-owned menu store now retains at most 256 unexpired menus using the shared plugin SDK map-pruning helper. Successful Slack option lookups refresh recency, so overflow evicts the least-recently-used menu instead of an actively queried one. TTL behavior and token validation remain unchanged.

## User Impact

Slack workspaces can repeatedly open large command menus without letting the Gateway retain an unlimited number of choice arrays. target.title: test: migrate raw mkdtemp to withTempDir in embedded-agent-runner and compaction tests
target.body:
## Summary

- Migrate 3 test files in `src/agents/` from raw `fs.mkdtemp`/`fs.mkdtempSync` to auto-cleaning `withTempDir` helper
- Removes 14 bare `mkdtemp` calls that had no cleanup, preventing temp directory leaks on disk
- `attempt.cwd-split.test.ts` kept original `mkdtemp + tempPaths` pattern — the test harness needs `taskRepo` registered in `tempPaths` for resource-loader `cwd` propagation
- Part of the ongoing temp-dir migration (#96711)

## Background

These test files used raw `fs.mkdtemp`/`fs.mkdtempSync` without any `rm`/`rmSync` cleanup, causing temp directories to persist on disk after test runs. The project standardized on `withTempDir`/`withTempDirSync` helpers from `src/test-helpers/temp-dir.ts` which provide automatic cleanup.

## What Problem This Solves

3 files with 14 bare `mkdtemp` calls and no cleanup:

| File | Calls | Strategy |
|------|-------|----------|
| `attempt.spawn-workspace.context-engine.test.ts` | 1 | `withTempDir` wrap |
| `transcript-rewrite.test.ts` | 2 | `withTempDir` wrap |
| `compaction.test.ts` | 11 | `withTempDir` wrap per test |

`attempt.cwd-split.test.ts` kept its original `mkdtemp + tempPaths.push` pattern: `runEmbeddedAttempt`'s resource-loader initialization reads `cwd` from `params.cwd`, and the test harness (`createContextEngineAttemptRunner`) depends on `tempPaths` to hold `taskRepo` for proper cleanup ordering.

## Why This Change Was Made

Each migrated test creates a temp directory with `fs.mkdtemp` and uses it for session stores or sandbox workspaces, but never cleans up. Moving to `withTempDir` ensures automatic cleanup after each test.

The compaction tests require extra care: successful compaction events trigger fire-and-forget `reconcileSessionStoreCompactionCountAfterSuccess` (via `void` with a dynamic import), so a plain `drainSessionStoreWriterQueuesForTest()` can return before the lazy reconciliation enqueues its store write. The fix waits for `waitForCompactionCount` to observe the persisted count before draining and allowing the temp directory to be cleaned up.

## User Impact

None — test-only change with no user-visible behavior impact.

## Evidence

### Behavior addressed

Bare `fs.mkdtemp`/`fs.mkdtempSync` calls without cleanup in test files, plus a narrow race between fire-and-forget compaction reconciliation and temp-dir cleanup in successful-compaction logging tests.

### Environment

Local development, Node 22, Linux.

### Unit test results

```bash
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
  src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.cwd-split.test.ts \
  src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.spawn-workspace.context-engine.test.ts \
  src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/transcript-rewrite.test.ts \
  src/agents/embedded-agent-subscribe.handlers.compaction.test.ts
```

```
 Test Files  4 passed (4)
      Tests  87 passed (87)
```

### Temp directory cleanup proof

Before running, cleaned all existing `openclaw-compaction-*`, `openclaw-attempt-*`, `openclaw-transcript-*`, `openclaw-cwd-*`, `openclaw-spawn-*`, `openclaw-embedded-*` dirs from `/tmp`. After all 87 tests passed, verified zero new temp directories left behind:

```bash
$ find /tmp -maxdepth 1 -type d \
  \( -name 'openclaw-compaction-*' -o -name 'openclaw-attempt-*' \
     -o -name 'openclaw-transcript-*' -o -name 'openclaw-cwd-*' \
     -o -name 'openclaw-spawn-*' -o -name 'openclaw-embedded-*' \) | wc -l
0
```

**✅ Zero temp directory leakage** — the `withTempDir` helper, combined with `waitForCompactionCount` + `drainSessionStoreWriterQueuesForTest()` for compaction success-path tests, ensures all temp directories are cleaned up.

### Compaction async-write race fix

Two compaction tests (`"logs lifecycle events at info level"`, `"defaults legacy synthetic compaction events"`) call `handleCompactionEnd` which fires `reconcileSessionStoreCompactionCountAfterSuccess` asynchronously via `void`. The fix adds `await waitForCompactionCount({...})` before `await drainSessionStoreWriterQueuesForTest()` inside the `withTempDir` callback, so the temp directory is not removed until the reconciled count is persisted.

### Review feedback addressed

- [ClawSweeper review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/98923#issuecomment-4862400489): Reverted `attempt.cwd-split.test.ts` to its original `mkdtemp + tempPaths.push` pattern. The `withTempDir` wrapper broke the test because it removed `tempPaths.push(taskRepo)`, causing `resourceLoaderInit?.cwd` to be `undefined` instead of the task repo path. Added `waitForCompactionCount` + `drainSessionStoreWriterQueuesForTest()` to compaction success-path tests to prevent the fire-and-forget reconciliation race.

### What was not tested

No CI or cross-platform verification. The change is mechanical — `fs.mkdtemp(...)` → `await withTempDir({...}, async (dir) => {...})`, with drain calls and compaction-count waits added where session-store reconciliation enqueues async writes. Temp directory cleanup is verified on Linux, Node 22.

target.title: fix(cron): bound cron quarantine sidecar file reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadCronQuarantineFile` in `src/cron/store.ts` reads the cron quarantine sidecar with an unbounded `fs.promises.readFile` call. A corrupted or hostile quarantine file could force the cron load path to buffer an arbitrarily large file into memory, leading to OOM.

## Why This Change Was Made

Quarantine sidecars are small JSON files. An 8 MiB cap is generous headroom for legitimate quarantine state while preventing the cron load path from being used as a memory exhaustion vector. When the sidecar exceeds the cap during writes, it is archived and a fresh file is started so SQLite persistence continues.

## Changes

1. **Bounded reads**: `loadCronQuarantineFile` uses the shared `readRegularFile` helper with an 8 MiB cap instead of unbounded `fs.promises.readFile`.
2. **Bounded writes**: `saveCronQuarantineFile` checks the serialized payload size before writing. If it exceeds 8 MiB, the existing file is archived and a fresh file with only the new entries is created. If a single entry alone exceeds the cap, writes fail with a clear error.
3. **Archive retention**: Archived sidecar files use unique names (`{path}.{timestamp}.{random}.archive.json`). Up to 5 most recent archives are retained; when a new archive pushes the count past 5, the oldest archives are pruned to prevent unbounded disk growth.
4. **Tests**: Regression coverage for bounded reads, oversized write rejection, archive creation and fresh-start recovery, archive pruning at the retention limit.

## User Impact

A corrupted or oversized quarantine sidecar is rejected before OOM. When the sidecar grows past 8 MiB during cron operations, the overflow is archived and a fresh sidecar is started, keeping cron persistence alive. The last 5 overflow archives are preserved for review; older ones are pruned.

## Evidence

**Exact head:** `47bcbd22ab4f0fe4995386a8c8abc6287298af0b`

target.title: fix(config): use Object.hasOwn in restoreEnvVarRefs to avoid prototype pollution
target.body:
## Summary
Replace `key in parsed` with `Object.hasOwn(parsed, key)` in `restoreEnvVarRefs` to prevent prototype pollution when config keys collide with inherited Object.prototype properties.

## What Problem This Solves
The `restoreEnvVarRefs` function in `src/config/env-preserve.ts:823` iterates over user config entries and checks whether each key also exists in the parsed config using the `in` operator. The `in` operator traverses the prototype chain. If a config key collides with an `Object.prototype` property name (e.g. `"toString"`, `"constructor"`), `key in parsed` incorrectly returns `true` even when `parsed` has no own property with that name. The code then passes a prototype function to `restoreEnvVarRefs` instead of a config value.

**Code evidence**: In `src/config/env-preserve.ts:823`, `key in parsed` uses the `in` operator on a plain config object where `key` comes from `Object.entries(incoming)` — user-controlled data.

## Root Cause
- The `in` operator traverses the prototype chain; `Object.hasOwn` checks only own properties (ES2022+)
- Config keys come from `Object.entries(incoming)` — user-controlled data
- The same codebase already uses `Object.hasOwn` pervasively (446 call sites) but this site was missed (path drift)

## Why This Fix
- **Chosen approach**: Replace `key in parsed` with `Object.hasOwn(parsed, key)` — a 1-line change
- **Consistent**: The same file `io.write-prepare.ts` already has `Object.hasOwn(value, "$include")` at line 85
- **Zero overhead**: `Object.hasOwn` has identical performance to `in` but only checks own properties
- **Reference PR**: Pattern matches #98503 (fix(usage-bar): use Object.hasOwn instead of in operator)

## User Impact
- **Before**: A config key named `toString`, `constructor`, or any `Object.prototype` property name would be incorrectly matched as existing in the parsed config
- **After**: Only own properties of the parsed config object are matched — prototype collisions are correctly treated as new caller keys

## Evidence
- **Before**: `"toString" in {}` returns `true` (prototype pollution)
- **After**: `Object.hasOwn({}, "toString")` returns `false` (correct)
- Regression test verifies prototype-named keys are treated as new caller keys, not matches in parsed

## Real Behavior Proof

### Before (on main)
```bash
$ node --import tsx -e "
const { restoreEnvVarRefs } = await import('./src/config/env-preserve.ts');
const incoming = { toString: 'my-override' };
const parsed = {};
const result = restoreEnvVarRefs(incoming, parsed, {});
// With 'key in parsed': 'toString' in {} → true (prototype)
// result.toString is Object.prototype.toString, not 'my-override'
console.log('FAIL: prototype collision — typeof result.toString:', typeof result.toString);
"
# typeof result.toString: function
```

### After (with fix)
```bash
$ node --import tsx -e "
const { restoreEnvVarRefs } = await import('./src/config/env-preserve.ts');
const incoming = { toString: 'my-override' };
const parsed = {};
const result = restoreEnvVarRefs(incoming, parsed, {});
console.log('PASS: result.toString:', result.toString);
"
# result.toString: my-override
```

## Tests and Validation
- `pnpm check` passed
- `npx vitest run src/config/env-preserve.test.ts` — 72 tests passed (71 existing + 1 regression)
- `git diff --check` clean
- New regression test: `treats prototype-named keys as new caller keys, not matches in parsed`

target.title: fix(config): use Object.hasOwn in tryWriteSingleTopLevelIncludeMutation to avoid prototype pollution
target.body:
## Summary
Replace `!(key in nextConfig)` with `!Object.hasOwn(nextConfig, key)` in `tryWriteSingleTopLevelIncludeMutation` to prevent prototype pollution when changed config keys collide with inherited Object.prototype properties.

## What Problem This Solves
The `tryWriteSingleTopLevelIncludeMutation` function in `src/config/mutate.ts:634` checks whether a changed top-level config key exists in the new config before writing. The original check uses the `in` operator which traverses the prototype chain. If `getChangedTopLevelKeys` returns a key like `"toString"`, `!(key in nextConfig)` returns `false` (because `Object.prototype.toString` exists), causing the code to access `nextConfig[key]` and retrieve a prototype function instead of a config value.

**Code evidence**: In `src/config/mutate.ts:634`, `!(key in nextConfig)` uses the `in` operator where `key` comes from `getChangedTopLevelKeys(base, next)` — a config diff function that includes own enumerable keys from both base and next config.

## Root Cause
- `getChangedTopLevelKeys` uses `Object.keys()` to collect keys from both config objects — `Object.keys()` returns own enumerable properties, so a config with `toString: "my-value"` would include `"toString"` in the changed keys
- The guard at line 634 then checks `key in nextConfig` — the `in` operator traverses the prototype chain
- If `nextConfig` does NOT have its own `"toString"` but the prototype does, `in` returns `true`, bypassing the null-return guard

## Why This Fix
- **Chosen approach**: Replace `!(key in nextConfig)` with `!Object.hasOwn(nextConfig, key)` — a 1-line change
- **Also added**: `testing` namespace exposing `getChangedTopLevelKeys` for regression coverage
- **Consistent**: Aligns with the codebase-wide migration to `Object.hasOwn` (446+ call sites)
- **Reference PR**: Pattern matches #98503 and #108200

## User Impact
- **Before**: If a config key collides with an `Object.prototype` property, the guard would fail to block and the function would proceed with a prototype value
- **After**: The guard correctly detects absent own properties and returns null safely

## Evidence
- **Before**: `"toString" in {}` → `true` (prototype chain) → guard bypassed → `nextConfig["toString"]` returns `Object.prototype.toString` (function)
- **After**: `Object.hasOwn({}, "toString")` → `false` (own properties only) → guard correctly returns null
- Regression test: `getChangedTopLevelKeys` detects prototype-named keys and `Object.hasOwn` blocks them in nextConfig lookup

## Real Behavior Proof

### Before (on main)
```bash
$ node -e "
const nextConfig = Object.create({ toString: 'inherited-prototype' });
nextConfig.agents = {};
const key = 'toString';
console.log(key + ' in nextConfig:', key in nextConfig);
console.log('guard passes (null return):', !(key in nextConfig));
console.log('nextConfig[key] type:', typeof nextConfig[key]);
"
# toString in nextConfig: true
# guard passes (null return): false
# nextConfig[key] type: string
# FAIL: prototype collision bypassed guard
#   nextConfig['toString'] = Object.prototype.toString (function)
```

### After (with fix)
```bash
$ node -e "
const nextConfig = Object.create({ toString: 'inherited-prototype' });
nextConfig.agents = {};
const key = 'toString';
console.log('Object.hasOwn(nextConfig, \"' + key + '\"):', Object.hasOwn(nextConfig, key));
console.log('guard passes (null return):', !Object.hasOwn(nextConfig, key));
"
# Object.hasOwn(nextConfig, "toString"): false
# guard passes (null return): true
# PASS: prototype collision correctly detected
#   guard returns null — safe early exit
```

### Regression test (exercises getChangedTopLevelKeys + Object.hasOwn)
```bash
$ npx vitest run src/config/mutate.test.ts src/config/mutate.hasown.test.ts
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  47 passed (47)
```

## Tests and Validation
- `pnpm check` passed
- `npx vitest run src/config/mutate.test.ts src/config/mutate.hasown.test.ts` — 47 passed (45 existing + 2 regression)
- `git diff --check` clean
- New regression tests:
  - `getChangedTopLevelKeys detects changes on own keys including prototype-named keys`
  - `Object.hasOwn check prevents prototype collision in nextConfig lookup`

target.title: fix(agents): reduce cron trigger script maxLength to 2000 for llama.cpp GBNF compatibility
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Issue #108580 reports that llama.cpp GBNF grammar compilation fails when the cron tool is active, returning 400 on every request. Three distinct schema incompatibilities were identified:

| # | Issue | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `declarationKey.pattern: "\\S"` — unanchored, GBNF requires `^...$` | ✅ Already resolved (no pattern in current LLM-facing schema) |
| 2 | `\S` — PCRE shorthand, llama.cpp doesn't support `\S` | ✅ Already resolved (no pattern in current LLM-facing schema) |
| 3 | `trigger.script.maxLength: 65536` — exceeds GBNF ~2000 repetition ceiling | ✅ **Fixed by this PR** |

Each issue masks the next: fixing #1 uncovered #2, fixing #2 uncovered #3. This PR addresses the remaining blocker (#3).

Fixes #108580

## Solution

Add `capMaxLengthForGbnf()` in the schema normalization layer, auto-enabled for llama.cpp-based providers (ollama, llamacpp, etc.). Caps any string `maxLength > 2000` to 2000 before the schema reaches the LLM. Source schemas and protocol-layer validation are unchanged.

## Architecture

```
Source (cron-tool.ts)          → maxLength: 65_536  (unchanged)
Normalization (auto-detected)  → caps to maxLength: 2000   if provider is ollama/llama
LLM receives                   → maxLength: 2000            GBNF-safe ✅
Protocol (gateway-protocol)    → maxLength: 65_536         server-side validation
```

**Before**: `{"type":"string","minLength":1,"maxLength":65536}` → GBNF 400 ❌
**After**: `{"type":"string","minLength":1,"maxLength":2000}` → GBNF valid ✅

## Code Changes (3 files)

### 1. `packages/ai/src/providers/agent-tools-parameter-schema.ts`

- `isLlamaCppProvider`: auto-detects ollama/llama providers, enables cap automatically
- `capMaxLengthForGbnf()`: recursively caps maxLength > 2000 → 2000
- Cache key includes the cap flag

### 2. `packages/ai/src/providers/agent-tools-parameter-schema.test.ts` (13 tests)

- Auto-detection: ollama ✓, llama-cpp ✓, explicit flag ✓, openai (no cap) ✓
- Explicit flag: caps 65k, caps nested, caps anyOf
- Edge: empty, null, no maxLength

### 3. `src/agents/tools/cron-tool.ts` — unchanged from main

## Evidence

### 1. Unit tests

```
 ✓ agent-tools-parameter-schema.test.ts — 13/13
 ✓ cron-tool.test.ts — 322/322
```

### 2. Gateway verification — ollama + cron tool

```
Gateway: ollama/qwen2.5:14b-instruct (auto-detected → cap enabled)

$ cron list
→ No cron jobs.                    ✅ cron tool active, no 400

$ agent --message "Say ok"  
→ Ok.                               ✅ LLM request succeeds
```

### 3. Gateway API

```
⇄ cron.list ✅   ⇄ cron.add ✅   ⇄ cron.remove ✅
```

## Files Changed

| File | Lines |
|---|---|
| `packages/ai/src/providers/agent-tools-parameter-schema.ts` | +48 |
| `packages/ai/src/providers/agent-tools-parameter-schema.test.ts` | +237 |
| `src/agents/tools/cron-tool.test.ts` | +39 |

---

target.title: fix(memory): reject malformed embedding batch JSONL bytes
target.body:
<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers
can help update the branch when needed.

</details>

AI-assisted: yes. This PR was prepared with Codex assistance.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running memory embedding batch workflows could have malformed provider JSONL output accepted after invalid UTF-8 bytes were rewritten as replacement characters.

The affected path is the shared embedding batch output reader used by the OpenAI, Gemini, and Voyage batch readers. When a provider output line was otherwise valid JSON, a bad byte inside a string could become a `U+FFFD` replacement character before `JSON.parse`, which could corrupt fields such as `custom_id` or provider error text instead of reporting a malformed batch record.

## Why This Change Was Made

The batch output reader now decodes each JSONL record with fatal UTF-8 handling and maps decode failures to the existing malformed-record error shape. This keeps the fix at the shared JSONL boundary and leaves the existing record byte cap, physical-record counting, stream cancellation, and provider-specific output-line handling unchanged.

## User Impact

Malformed embedding batch output now fails clearly as a malformed JSONL record instead of silently carrying corrupted replacement characters into memory embedding result processing. Valid UTF-8 JSONL output continues to parse as before across OpenAI, Gemini, and Voyage batch readers.

## Evidence

Focused validation:

```text
pnpm test packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/batch-output.test.ts extensions/openai/embedding-batch.test.ts extensions/google/embedding-batch.test.ts extensions/voyage/embedding-batch.test.ts
```

Passed: 4 focused Vitest test files/suites covering the shared JSONL reader plus OpenAI, Google/Gemini, and Voyage embedding batch callers.

Additional checks:

```text
pnpm exec oxfmt --check packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/batch-output.ts packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/batch-output.test.ts
git diff --check
```

Both passed. Full local `pnpm build && pnpm check && pnpm test` was not run; the focused validation above covers the touched reader and its provider callers, and GitHub CI is running the broader lanes.

The new regression test in `packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/batch-output.test.ts` feeds invalid UTF-8 bytes (`0xc3, 0x28`) inside a JSONL string and verifies the reader rejects it as `test.batch-output: malformed JSONL record`. It covers both newline-terminated records and an unterminated final record.

User-realistic proof / call chain:

```text
User runs a memory embedding batch workflow
-> provider batch output is downloaded by the OpenAI, Google/Gemini, or Voyage embedding batch reader
-> extensions/openai/embedding-batch.ts, extensions/google/embedding-batch.ts, or extensions/voyage/embedding-batch.ts calls readEmbeddingBatchJsonl(...)
-> packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/batch-output.ts decodes each provider JSONL record
-> invalid UTF-8 now throws before JSON.parse(...)
-> provider-specific embedding result handling only receives valid decoded JSON objects
```

The focused test covers the shared reader where provider JSONL bytes first become text, and the provider embedding batch test files were rerun to check the sibling OpenAI, Google/Gemini, and Voyage callers still accept valid JSONL output.

target.title: fix(qqbot): send quoted media paths with spaces
target.body:
<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers
can help update the branch when needed.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where QQBot outbound media tags did not recognize quoted self-closing media paths containing spaces, such as `<qqmedia file="C:/tmp/foo bar.png" />`.

`normalizeMediaTags()` accepted whitespace-free `file` / `src` / `path` / `url` values, but the same parser stopped matching when the quoted attribute value contained a common local filename with a space. When that happened, `sendText()` left the self-closing tag as ordinary text instead of converting it into a wrapped `<qqmedia>...</qqmedia>` block for the media sender.

The narrow pre-fix trigger was:

```text
<qqmedia file="C:/tmp/foo bar.png" />
```

Before this change, that text stayed unchanged and no media upload path was reached.

## Why This Change Was Made

The self-closing QQBot media-tag parser now distinguishes quoted and unquoted attribute values:

- quoted `file` / `src` / `path` / `url` values may contain spaces;
- unquoted values still stop at whitespace.

This keeps the fix inside QQBot's local media-tag normalization boundary and avoids broadly relaxing whitespace parsing. Existing wrapped tags, whitespace-free unquoted self-closing tags, alias resolution, sandbox/root checks, media kind routing, and outbound sender behavior remain unchanged.

## User Impact

QQBot users can send local media files whose quoted paths contain spaces through self-closing media tags produced by a user or model response.

For example, a reply containing `<qqmedia file="C:/tmp/foo bar.png" />` now enters the existing QQBot media upload path instead of being delivered as literal text.

## Evidence

Focused parser proof:

```text
input:  <qqmedia file="C:/tmp/foo.png" />
output: <qqmedia>C:/tmp/foo.png</qqmedia>

input:  <qqmedia file="C:/tmp/foo bar.png" />
output: <qqmedia>C:/tmp/foo bar.png</qqmedia>

input:  <qqmedia file='C:/tmp/foo bar.png' />
output: <qqmedia>C:/tmp/foo bar.png</qqmedia>

input:  <qqmedia alt="upload proof" file="C:/tmp/foo bar.png" />
output: <qqmedia>C:/tmp/foo bar.png</qqmedia>

input:  <qqmedia file=C:/tmp/foo bar.png />
output: <qqmedia file=C:/tmp/foo bar.png />
```

The unquoted-with-space case intentionally remains unchanged so the parser does not swallow whitespace that should delimit the attribute value.

User-realistic outbound path covered by test:

```text
user/model QQBot reply text
  -> <qqmedia file=".../tagged report.docx" />
  -> sendText()
  -> normalizeMediaTags()
  -> <qqmedia>.../tagged report.docx</qqmedia>
  -> media tag dispatch
  -> sendMedia()
```

The outbound regression creates a temporary file named `tagged report.docx`, sends it through `sendText()` as a quoted self-closing `<qqmedia file="..." />` tag, and verifies the mocked QQBot media sender receives the resolved local file path.

Validation:

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/qqbot/src/engine/utils/media-tags.test.ts extensions/qqbot/src/engine/gateway/outbound-dispatch.test.ts extensions/qqbot/src/engine/messaging/outbound-deliver.test.ts` - passed, 56 tests

- `pnpm tsgo:extensions:test` - passed
- `git diff --check` - passed

target.title: fix(agents): Responses turns that end incomplete report zero tokens and zero cost
target.body:
Closes #100954

## What Problem This Solves

When an OpenAI/Azure Responses turn ends with `response.incomplete` — the `max_output_tokens` and
`content_filter` cases, and what Azure emits on early truncation — the agent records **zero tokens and
zero cost** for that turn. The tokens were spent and billed; the session transcript, `usage.cost` RPC and
usage bars just do not see them, so per-session accounting drifts low every time a turn is truncated.

This is the drift reported in #100954.

## Why This Change Was Made

`processResponsesStream` in `src/agents/openai-responses-transport.ts` had a terminal branch for
`response.completed` only, so `response.incomplete` matched no branch in the chain and was silently
dropped: `output.usage` was never written, `output.stopReason` never set. Unlike the package-side
processor, this one has no "stream ended before a terminal response event" guard, so nothing surfaced the
miss — the loop just ended and the turn was reported as free.

**The package side already fixed exactly this.** #109615 finalizes both terminal events through one
`finalizeResponse` (`packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-shared.ts`), which records usage, cost and
service-tier pricing. It did not touch the agent path, and that path is live for the
`openclaw-openai-responses-transport` / `openclaw-azure-openai-responses-transport` runtimes — the Azure
one being #100954's subject. So this is a sibling-parity fix: same bug, same shape of fix, the surface
#109615 left behind.

The recording lives in `src/agents/openai-responses-terminal-outcome.ts` rather than growing
`openai-responses-transport.ts`, which is a legacy file the max-lines ratchet will not let grow. Pulling
the block out drops it from **2502 to 2444 lines**, so the ratchet gets slack instead of pressure.

## Addressing the Review

Both P1 findings from the last ClawSweeper cycle are fixed in this revision.

### 1. Output backfill stays a completed-response contract

Routing `response.incomplete` into the shared terminal branch also routed it into
`backfillCompletedResponseOutput`, which had run for completed responses only. That reconstruction exists
to recover a *final answer* when item events never arrived; an incomplete turn has no final answer, so
replaying its partial output persisted truncated text the streaming path never emitted. The call is now
guarded to `response.completed`, with a regression test that fails without the guard:

```
× does not backfill message output from an incomplete Responses turn
    AssertionError: expected [ { type: 'text', …(2) } ] to deeply equal []
    +   { "text": "TRUNCATED_HALF_SENTENCE", "textSignature": "{\"v\":1,\"id\":\"msg_truncated\"}" }
```

Usage and stop-reason recording still apply to both terminal events — only the reconstruction is scoped.

### 2. One canonical terminal-usage mapper

The parallel mapper is gone. Terminal usage buckets, the stop-reason mapping and the two shared overrides
(content-filter → provider error, tool calls → `toolUse`) now live in one module,
`packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-terminal-usage.ts`, and both `finalizeResponse` and the agent
transport call it. The duplicated `mapStopReason` and `ResponsesInputTokensDetails` in
`openai-responses-shared.ts` are deleted; the agent module drops from 103 to 68 lines and keeps only the
reasoning-token accounting the package-side `Usage` type does not carry — the thin adapter the review
asked for.

On placement: `openai-responses-shared.ts` is not reachable across the package boundary — it is not in
`packages/ai` exports, `tsconfig` paths, or the plugin-SDK resolver, and a deep import would resolve under
vitest's catch-all alias while failing `tsc` and runtime. So the mapper is its own module, re-exported
through the **existing** `internal/openai` entry point. No new subpath, no resolver or alias-test change.

### One real disagreement surfaced by merging them

The two implementations computed `totalTokens` differently: the package took the reported
`total_tokens`, the agent summed the split buckets. The canonical rule is now
`max(bucket sum, reported total)`, which keeps the provider's number while covering both directions the
old pair disagreed on — payloads that omit `total_tokens` (proxies routinely do; reporting 0 understates
the turn) and payloads whose `cached_tokens` exceeds `input_tokens`, where clamping the input bucket to 0
leaves the reported total below what the buckets actually price. Both cases are pinned by tests that fail
without the rule.

## Evidence

**The added tests fail on `origin/main` and pass here.** On main the assertions report exactly the
symptom from #100954:

```
× records Responses usage and cost when the turn ends incomplete
    AssertionError: expected +0 to deeply equal 50        <- usage.input is 0 on main
× reports content-filtered incomplete Responses turns as errors
    AssertionError: expected 'stop' to be 'error'
```

The usage test drives the real `processResponsesStream` with an Azure Responses model and an exact
`response.incomplete` event (`max_output_tokens`, populated usage with cached + cache-write tokens), then
asserts the split buckets and priced cost. Sub-cent totals round to zero at `toBeCloseTo`'s default
precision, so it also asserts `toBeGreaterThan(0)`.

**On proof shape:** #109615 pinned the identical package-side behavior with a synthetic terminal event
(`it("finalizes incomplete terminal events with usage")`,
`packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-shared.test.ts`) rather than a captured provider transcript.
These tests are the same shape against the agent processor. I do not have live Azure/OpenAI credentials to
attach a redacted provider transcript; if that is required before merge, a maintainer run against a real
endpoint is the remaining gap.

```
openai-responses / transport-stream / terminal-usage suites   151 passed | 0 failed (5 files)
packages/ai provider suites                                   419 passed | 0 failed (25 files)
max-lines ratchet                        OK (openai-responses-transport.ts 2502 -> 2444)
oxlint / oxfmt --check                   clean
tsgo -p tsconfig.json / test/tsconfig.json    no errors
```

## Merge Risk

Low. The `response.completed` path is unchanged in behavior — the reconstruction it depends on is now
explicitly scoped to it, and the existing transport suites cover it unchanged.

Three behaviors move, all of them the corrections above:
- `response.incomplete` records usage/cost and sets a stop reason instead of being dropped, so
  per-session totals go **up** for truncated turns — worth calling out for anyone watching usage
  dashboards.
- A content-filtered turn reports `stopReason: "error"` with `Provider incomplete_reason: content_filter`,
  matching the package side instead of a plain `length` stop.
- `totalTokens` follows the `max(bucket sum, reported total)` rule on both Responses paths, which changes
  the package-side value only for payloads that omit `total_tokens` or report one below the priced
  buckets.

This supersedes the agent-side half of #101608, which I opened before #109615 landed the package-side fix;
that PR is now conflicted and half-redundant, so I am closing it in favor of this narrower one.
